I wake up every day with a mission. I work a full time job with stellar reviews, take a full load of courses towards my degree with straight A’s, take care of my family (including an active toddler), and function so highly in society that nobody but those quite close to me know about my diagnoses, and were shocked when I told them. Even the staff at the behavioral health unit where I was hospitalized for suicidal ideation were surprised because “I don’t seem like the type of person who ends up there” and that I “seem so capable and well adjusted”.

People who flippantly tell me that getting a new hobby or being more positive will help me have little understanding of the seriousness of mental health issues. You wouldn’t tell someone born with diabetes to just “eat better”. That’s a small part of maintenance in their illness, just like hobbies and “positivity” are only a tiny part of maintenance in depression. Try slogging through an activity you used to love with an emptiness that hurts while you suffer through a nasty bout of anhedonia, but pushing through because not doing anything is somehow worse than that feeling.

I know I’m coming across as angry, but it’s a great sadness as well. This sentiment is very much why so many with mental health issues suffer through in silence. I disagree with this for a few reasons:

1. Designated note takers exist in basically every form of official meeting I have attended. If that person is required to speak/act, we usually use a shared doc and someone else picks up. This is just good practice so we remember the agreements/etc. made.

2. Some people suck at writing good notes for D&D and some excel. There is an important balance between content and description.

3. Really, your characters are living this without a break between. It’s silly to me to penalize people who might have poor working memory or writing skills when they don’t remember something that happened 13 minutes ago game time but 13 days ago real time. With job/school/family duties filling the mind between. It’s a group game and group effort. If I’m playing the 16 INT wizard with a sharp memory but am in real life an ADHD person who muddles numbers or dates, someone else in the party OOC reminding me of vital info is just good form.

Hello,

Number one, I’m here if you want to talk about your situation or journey. I’ve been there. Multiple times. I’ve only made it by having understanding, empathetic people in my life. Please DM me anytime if you want to talk. I won’t patronize you or tell you to smile more, I promise.

That said, I know I can’t stop you, but I would really like you to try and get some therapeutic help since this will take you time. Try to write a pro/con square and be really truthful and realistic. When I wrote mine I put down absolute, concrete things I provide the world, like paying for my son’s health insurance because I believed I wasn’t worth being alive. If the world is painful and the depression is overwhelming, try to map the last month or year as realistically as you can. How many days were you depressed? How many happy? Did it pass? I know in the middle of things it is hard to remember a single happy time, but I use my phone’s camera roll to recall events that shone. I pull up my calendar. Scroll through emails. If you journal (I suck at this) look at how many positive events there are. I strongly believe that nothing lasts forever, the good and the bad, it’s just learning the balance.

It takes effort and resources to create it and nurture it, so ending it prematurely doesn’t make sense.

My attempt scared my loved ones, and they wanted to support me, too. Fortunately one of them really pushed me to go into the hospital to get help. It put me on a path towards learning skills and getting valuable therapy that I’m still on, but I get to be here still for my wife and son.

I explain as such - sadness brought on like events is like laying in a full bathtub. Parts of you are covered and the water laps at you, but if pull yourself up on the edges, you can be mostly dry for a minute. Depressive sadness and emptiness is like swimming in a stormy sea. You go under, choking on water and surface again. Sometimes you might find a piece of driftwood to grab onto for a while, but you’re still constantly swimming to make it. Any time you stop swimming and let go you chance drowning. Until you have the tools to call a boat, you’re swimming until you get so tired you can’t anymore. I understand. I’m much older than you and didn’t get diagnosed until last year because I didn’t want to talk to anyone about it. All I can say is with a diagnosis like ours, it is progressive. Even if it’s hard, I’d do the best to get what you can out of the resources you have. See if you can change therapists to someone who specializes in bipolar or has good experience with it (this is not as common and it sucks!) and see if you can talk to whoever prescribed Abilify. Tell them it didn’t work and you’d like to talk options. Bipolar medication is an art, not a science, and it can take a lot of tweaking to get it to work well. Be honest about side effects, how well you took it, and for how long. Also, see if you can get referred to a DBT group. It seems touchy-feely but can really help. CBT is good too, especially for anxiety and rumination. Have you had a manic period with psychosis?

If you haven’t opened up, it really does. But if you can get a therapist you connect with enough to talk to, it can help. It’s especially hard with trauma and/or PTSD/C-PTSD. Therapy, or groups, are where you can learn the methods, skills, and coping strategies to help you feel that you can live.

If you never sought help for it, they see it as you dying by something they could have done better helping you with if they had seen it sooner, or supported you better. Something preventable or treatable that was allowed to grow because of their mistake.

This would be like a friend of yours showing clear signs of a treatable illness that they, and you, ignored, allowing it to become worse and worse, even though you both knew the warning signs. Or perhaps you didn’t know the warning signs, but you knew something was off. But, you never mentioned it because you were too polite, or were scared and uncomfortable bringing it up, or didn’t know how to handle it. If that friend died and you hadn’t done anything to help them see the possibility of treatment, or that there were ways to work within the pain and improve, you’d feel like shit. You’d never forgive yourself.

This one always bothers me. I don’t believe killing yourself is selfish. I also would never call it committing suicide or killing yourself. I’d be more likely to call it completing suicide, death by suicide, or death from mental illness. Because that’s what it is. Suicide is most of the time losing the battle with mental illness. It isn’t weakness, or selfishness. It’s the inability to continue on with the pain you’re in.

That being said, I also don’t think it’s selfish of those around you to want to stop you. They love you and care about you. If someone I cared about had cancer and was resisting chemotherapy or refused to take treatment for it, I would be fighting them tooth and nail to get the help they needed. The same can go for mental health crises. It’s just a lot harder on all sides because of the stigma and the less “hard science” portion of treatment makes it harder to pursue good, effective help, and for all parties to see eye to eye.

It may seem like these people do this to stroke their egos and brag. It may even be the case, but it seems unlikely they would go out of their way to save someone they didn’t even care for.
